The two dots on ü show that the u IS pronounced: vergüenza = “ber-GWEN-tha”, pingüino = “peen-GWEE-no”.
It’s linked: “se me olvidó” = “semeolbido”. Say it like one word.
1. “Se me olvidó”: it wasn’t my fault!
A brilliant construction: when something happens to you without meaning it, the thing becomes the subject and you are the “victim”. Literally “the pen forgot itself on me”.
The pen got forgotten on me.
A Mihai se le cayó la cartera.
The structure: SE + pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) + verb (agreeing with the thing: singular / plural).
The difference: “Rompí el vaso” = I broke the glass (maybe on purpose). “Se me rompió el vaso” = the glass broke on me (an accident!). Spaniards use the second one to say “it’s not my fault”.
2. General obligation: hay que, hace falta
It is necessary to make an appointment.
“Hay que” has no subject and isn’t conjugated: never “hay que yo…”. For a specific person use “tengo que”.
3. Possessive pronouns: el mío, la tuya
To say “mine, yours”, you use the article + mío / tuyo / suyo…, agreeing with the thing owned:
Is it your wallet? — Yes, it’s mine.
My car is red; yours is blue.
After SER, the article usually disappears: “Es mía” = It’s mine. “¿Es suya?” = Is it yours?
4. Someone / no one, something / nothing: the double negative
Unlike standard English, Spanish uses the DOUBLE NEGATIVE: “There isn’t anybody” = “No hay nadie” (literally “There isn’t nobody”).
“Alguno” and “ninguno” lose the -o before a masculine noun: algún día, ningún problema.

In Spain there’s no Friday the 13th. The unlucky day is Tuesday the 13th. As the saying goes: “On a Tuesday, don’t get married or set off on a journey.”
Tom didn’t believe in such things. Until that Tuesday, the 13th of October.
It all started at seven in the morning. He forgot to set his alarm and woke up at half past eight. He had a meeting at nine.
He got dressed in a rush. While he was drinking a coffee, he dropped the cup and stained his white shirt. He had to change.
He left the house and, as he closed the door, he realised something terrible: he’d left his keys inside.
“Never mind,” he thought. “Lena has a spare set.” But Lena was in Berlin, visiting her parents.
He got to the office at twenty past nine. The meeting had already started. His boss looked at him seriously.
When he wanted to present his project, the computer didn’t work. His charger had broken and the battery was at two per cent.
At lunchtime he went to eat at a restaurant near the office. He ordered a salad. The waiter brought him fish soup. Tom hates fish.
When he wanted to pay, he couldn’t find his wallet. He had left it in the other shirt… the one with the coffee stain.
Luckily, the waiter was very nice: “Don’t worry. You can pay me tomorrow.”
In the afternoon it started to rain. Tom didn’t have an umbrella, of course. He reached his building completely soaked and had to wait two hours for the locksmith.
At ten at night he finally got into his flat. He sat on the sofa, tired and in a bad mood. Then the phone rang.
It was his boss: “Tom, I’ve seen your project in my email. It’s excellent. We’re going to give you the director’s job.”
Tom sat in silence for a moment. Then he started to laugh. In the end, Tuesday the 13th hadn’t been so bad after all.
Since that day, every Tuesday the 13th, Tom carries an umbrella, two chargers and a spare set of keys in his backpack. Just in case.
